Number two: if you bypass number one and you're already in it, learn how to quit Amazon. There's no respect for human decency there. UPS drivers start at 28 dollars an hour and make 40 after a few years. FedEx drivers aren't far behind. Amazon drivers get paid the same as someone working at a pizza place. You're doing all the work of a UPS or FedEx driver getting paid pennies in comparison.

Everyone I've talked to that worked at Amazon has quit. Not fired, quit. And the people that have been fired should probably sue because they'd more than likely win.

Number three: work for somebody else. That's literally it, because if you work for somebody else you won't be working at Amazon and you'll be happy.

I've never seen anybody work at Amazon for more than two months. Also, Amazon will offer you a three thousand dollar signing bonus — read the fine print. It's spread over an 80 week period with a 30 day trial, so you only see a fraction of it.

Find somewhere else. Don't even entertain it. It's quite terrible, it's just not fun.

I worked at Amazon for three and a half years in the outbound department of a fulfillment center. These buildings are massive, around 17 football fields. I worked in the pac department and ship dock.

**Pros:**

The pay is decent, not great. Better than retail or fast food but for a company that size you'd expect more. They switched to weekly pay towards the end which was nice.

Insurance is really good — medical, dental and vision for less than 40 dollars a month as a single person. A lot of people worked there just for the insurance. They have a 401k with a match up to two percent, but the match doesn't vest for three years, meaning if you quit before three years you lose it. They don't make that obvious, you have to read the fine print.

Four day work week with three day weekends, but 10 hour shifts. I loved the three day weekends but work took up your whole day. I felt like my life was on pause for four days — wake up, work, eat, shower, sleep, repeat. No time to do anything else or you'd show up exhausted.

You don't deal with customers at all, everything is behind the scenes. I specifically looked for jobs like that.

Made a lot of friends there, which surprised me. Around a thousand employees between day and overnight shifts.

Time off was generous — vacation, PTO, and unpaid time off. After a year you had almost a full month off total. You manage it yourself through an app, no questions asked. Bad day? Walk out mid-shift, nobody says anything as long as you have time. However if you hit zero time you're automatically terminated, no second chances, your badge won't even let you in.

VTO — voluntary time off — was an option when it was slow. You could leave without pay but without using your time. Sometimes I walked in and within three minutes they were offering VTO. The downside is you can't predict it and you don't get paid.

Mandatory overtime when busy — up to 60 hours a week, six days. If you want money there's money to be made, but doing heavy lifting for 60 hours a week with only one day to rest is brutal.

**Cons:**

A lot of heavy lifting, very physically demanding for 10 hour shifts. After years of it your body is just done. Some tasks take 30 seconds and you repeat them for 10 hours straight. After one hour you realize you have nine more hours and then three more days after that.

Basically anyone gets hired. In my group interview the first thing they said was if you can pass a drug test and want any of these shifts you have a job. The drug test is a mouth swab and easy to get around. I'd predict 25 to 50 percent of the building would fail a full drug test.

Because anyone gets hired you get people doing as little work as possible. I once looked at numbers halfway through a shift — I'd done 500 boxes, the other two people did about 200 each. I wasn't even trying hard, just working at a normal pace. The bar is set so low that if you're capable they pile more work on you, and if you're not capable not much is expected. It's very unfair.

There were people called wannabe supervisors who realized supervisors do less physical work, so they'd walk around fast pretending to be in charge, bossing people around when they weren't. It was a joke.

I had a situation where I was scheduled for a half day of overtime. Last minute at the morning meeting they announced it was actually a full day. I went straight to HR and the rep gave me attitude, basically said too bad. I was so enraged I was cursing at her. The head of the building walked me back to HR, told me to work the half day and they'd sort it out. I worked the half day furious and left. Because I left I had to use six hours of my own time to cover the rest of the scheduled shift. Never got it back. That was the point where I thought why do I even try for this company.

Another time I hurt my back lifting. When I went to the safety office the very first thing they asked was whether I was lifting properly — trying to get me to admit fault so they weren't responsible. I told my supervisor my back was hurt and the very first thing out of their mouth was about the day's package numbers and whether their targets would be affected. Couldn't believe it.

They're supposed to rotate your job so you're not using the same muscles every day, but I'd end up doing the same task three out of four days constantly.

**Overall:** If you're coming from fast food or retail it's a step up. If you need real income for a family it probably won't cut it unless you move up to management, where the pay is actually decent. I personally had no interest in moving up — I was building my eBay business the whole time I was there. That's eventually why I quit.

I got hired at Amazon in August 2020. When you apply they let you pick whatever shift you want. I work Sunday night to Wednesday, off Thursday through Sunday. They also have donut shifts where you work Monday-Tuesday, off Wednesday, work Thursday-Friday, off the weekend. Lots of shift options.

After applying I got a response within 30 minutes to two hours — way faster than I expected. They send a ton of emails with your start date, pay rate, and pre-training documents with little tests. Complete all of it, they warned that not finishing by the due date could affect your hiring.

Orientation tip: get there early or you'll be stuck at the back of the line. The drug test is a cheek swab, nothing invasive. You get your badge photo taken the same day as the drug test so look decent for it.

The A to Z app is where you do everything — clock in, pick up shifts, request time off, see your pay and schedule. Amazon pays weekly.

**Time off breakdown:**
Personal time (PTO) — paid. Vacation — accumulates each paycheck but very slowly. Unpaid time — not paid but doesn't affect other balances. COVID time off — fully paid, I took a month off for COVID and got paid every week. Bereavement — three days off if you lose someone.

VTO is voluntary time off — they offer it when it's slow, you go home without pay but your other time balances are untouched. VET is voluntary extra time — you pick up extra shifts for extra pay, but once you accept you cannot back out. If you don't show up and don't have enough time to cover it you go negative and that's termination.

**Benefits are top tier** — health, dental, vision, 401k, stock options, and fully prepaid tuition as long as you stay with the company. Benefits start as soon as you walk in and sign up.

**Hair safety is serious.** Long hair must be tied up — a girl at my location had her hair pulled into a conveyor belt and lost her scalp. Put braids up, wear a bonnet, clip up wigs. Don't risk it.

Nails you can wear long but expect to break them. No nail policy enforced but it's on you.

Dress code is whatever you want — comfortable clothes, any shoes. They do offer a free pair of Zappos shoes up to 100 dollars. Wear them — steel toe protection matters because you can drop a tote on your foot at any time. My Pumas after two years are done.

Do I like Amazon? It's a job. It's paying my bills. The benefits alone make it worth it if you need coverage.

Pay in Virginia is $19 an hour, was $18.60 before a recent increase. First paycheck takes two weeks — they do that on purpose so people don't work one week and quit. We get paid every Wednesday.

Amazon is not a place for the weak. If you can't get through long shifts mentally, don't work there. The work itself isn't so bad, it's just the hours. Getting off at 4:30 or 5am is brutal. The only time I really enjoy my day is on my day off. By the six or seven hour mark of a shift you're already ready to leave, and leaving early costs you PTO so keep that in mind.

VTO comes up randomly — you can drop your shift with no consequences, just no pay. Take it fast because someone else will grab it immediately. They offer it when there's more workers than work to do.

Breaks are two 30 minute breaks, roughly at the 10 hour and 2am/2pm marks depending on your shift. 30 minutes sounds like a lot until you try to go get food — there's nothing within 15 minutes of my facility so you'd be gone 45 minutes minimum. Bring your own food.

Managers vary. Mine are mostly chill. Some are strict about earbuds and phones. Some are stricter about bathroom breaks than others — luckily mine aren't, but that depends on your department and building.

Overall would I recommend it? The pay is decent, the work itself isn't bad, it's just the 10 hour shifts. I personally wouldn't do it long term but if you want to build up savings or work toward a management career it's not a bad option. I'm using it part time to build money while I look for something else.

You do have to work some holidays like Thanksgiving and Christmas — I haven't hit that yet but it's coming up.

I found myself working at Amazon after needing steady income. Before starting I researched online and heard some scary stories, but a lot of those videos were titled "I worked at Amazon for one day" or "two days" — and orientation is two days long, so those people never actually did the job.

**Surviving orientation:** First two days are 10 hour orientation days sitting in a room. I was hoping for 6 or 8 hours — it's 10. Bring snacks, water, and gum to stay awake. They have free coffee and hot chocolate but vending machines add up fast.

**Your feet:** There is no job at Amazon that requires you to sit down. Everything is standing, including the forklift machines. Your feet will hurt badly for the first two to three weeks, especially when you get off shift — not so much while you're working but you feel the burn after. That pain goes away. Soak your feet in Epsom salt on your days off, do foot massages, take care of them. After two to three weeks your feet adjust and you can work overtime without feeling it. If you already have chronic foot problems, this is not the job for you.

Composite toe shoes are required for safety. Amazon gives you up to $100 credit through Zappos. Order early because they usually arrive before orientation. If they don't fit right they'll give you shoe covers in the meantime.

**The A to Z app** is everything — time off, vacation, PTO, UPT tracking, medical benefits, 401k, discounts. Learn it inside and out because it can be the difference between staying and leaving.

Career Choice inside the app is a huge deal. Free language classes for non-native English speakers. Free GED and high school diploma programs. College tuition paid after six months of employment — $5,000 per semester. Financial advisors to help with buying a home or starting a business. If you factor in $5,000 per semester that's $20,000 extra per year on top of your wages.

Benefits include dental that covers 50% even on cosmetic procedures, which is rare.

**Time off breakdown:** You earn about 50 minutes of UPT (unpaid time) per shift, so roughly 2 hours 50 minutes per week. About 1 hour 50 minutes of paid time off per week. Vacation accumulates separately. Your job is tied to your UPT — the moment you go negative you're at risk of immediate termination. Some facilities fire you the second you go negative. Never go negative. Treat your UPT like money and always know your balance.

Get the prepaid card from HR within your first couple days. It lets you access up to 50% of your pay from day one. If you need gas money or to pay a bill that first week before your paycheck clears, this covers it. Don't abuse it but it's there when you need it.

**Leadership:** Show up and do your job consistently. You don't have to suck up but just doing your work right every time gets you noticed. Amazon rewards trustworthy employees who don't need to be told how to do their job.

Pick a shift that actually works for you. Ten hours on a shift you hate is brutal. Night person? Pick nights. Don't let the shift eat your life.

Give the job a real chance before deciding to leave. A lot of people quit during orientation before ever doing the actual work. Check every resource in the app first because the true value of the job goes way beyond the hourly wage.

15 minute breaks I just go to my car to get some quiet since inside the warehouse is noisy. Lunch break is 30 minutes. There are three vending machines in the break room and they sell out fast.

The last hour of a double shift feels like it takes forever. Doing a 10 hour shift is not easy but they were paying the $3 premium so I pushed through it. Got home after being awake for 12 hours.

Overall Amazon is a somewhat okay place to work. I think it's a good part time job for extra cash, but it all depends on you.

Things I wish I knew before working at Amazon.

Your first day you're going to be sore unless your body is already used to physical activity. You're standing on your feet for 10 hours with two 30 minute breaks. Wear comfortable shoes. Amazon offers shoes through Zappos but the first pair I got wasn't comfortable — I had to break them in. The Zappos shoes are really designed for steel toe protection more than comfort. Amazon is very strict about protective footwear and will send you home if you show up without the right shoes. The socks that saved my life were Dr. Scholl's circulatory socks.

The hiring process is not a real interview. You show up with ID, prove citizenship, take a drug test and that's it. Pick your shift online and you basically already have the job unless you fail the background check or drug test. Amazon reportedly no longer tests for marijuana — I've heard this from many people who said they shouldn't have passed and did.

Get six to eight hours of sleep every night. Coming in unrested with 10 hours ahead of you makes everything miserable. Stay hydrated — Amazon has water coolers throughout the building with fresh cold water, no limits. Sip every 30 minutes rather than chugging so you don't feel full and sluggish.

Every station has a rate — a target amount of product to get out per shift. Don't focus on hitting rate every single second because it's technically nine hours of physical work and you'll burn out by midday. Find a consistent rhythm. What works for me is packing fast then giving myself a 30 second break, then going again. Check your rate every hour and adjust what's working.

No uniform but hair must be pulled back and not below your shoulders, shorts can't be above your fingertips, no spaghetti strap tops. Wear something loose and comfortable — you're in a warehouse and you will sweat.

Do not overdo overtime if you're not used to physical work. The three days off you get each week are genuinely needed for your body to recover. Maximum is 60 hours a week and they'll send you home when you approach that. Burning yourself out on overtime means you'll start missing your regular shifts and your UPT will drain fast. You get 80 hours of unpaid time — when it hits negative you're fired.

Every so often the screens stop and give you two 15 second stretch breaks — back stretches, hamstring stretches, even breathing exercises if you're having a rough day. Ergonomic mats at your station also help a lot if you have foot or back problems.

Two 30 minute breaks — the first is unpaid, the second is paid. Do not go over on that second break. It's tracked scan-to-scan, not by clocking in and out. The timer starts on the last item you scan before break and ends on the first item you scan when you return. I went over by about 7 to 12 minutes and got a write-up. Nobody told me about this during orientation.

Amazon discounts only apply to actual Amazon products shipped from Amazon buildings, not third party sellers. Nine times out of ten what you're looking at isn't an Amazon product so don't count on discounts.

If you're a social butterfly this might be hard. You're assigned to a station alone and focused on hitting rate, so there's not much time to talk except at lunch. A lot of people say it feels depressing because of the isolation. That said, talk to people when you can — coworkers will fill you in on things orientation left out and help you avoid getting written up.

A lot of Amazon's rules you won't find out about until you get in trouble for them. Pay attention and ask questions early.
